answer.line: Halfway to equivalence, [A^-] = [HA], so pH = pKa = 4.74.

steps: Start from what halfway means: half the acetic acid is now acetate, so [A^-] = [HA].
Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log([A^-]/[HA]) = pKa + log 1 = pKa.
pKa = -log(1.8 x 10^-5). That K_a sits between 10^-5 and 10^-4, so pKa is between 4 and 5. Only 4.74 fits.

choices.note: This is the pH before any NaOH goes in: 0.100 M acetic acid alone. A real point on the curve, at another moment.
The halfway point sits mid-buffer, where acid and conjugate base are equal.
pH 7 at equivalence is the strong acid, strong base case. Here pH 7 comes just before equivalence, and halfway you are in the buffer.
At equivalence every HA has become A^-, a weak base, so the pH sits above 7. That is 8.72. The stem asks about halfway.
14 - 4.74 = 9.26 is the pKb of acetate. The buffer equation for the acid uses pKa.

lockIt: At the half-equivalence point of a weak acid titration, pH = pKa.

video.title: Reading a weak acid titration curve

visual.reuse: new small plotter; the curve is computed from the parameters by exact charge balance, so each mark lands on the true curve
visual.alt: Titration curve of 25.0 mL of 0.100 M acetic acid with 0.100 M NaOH: pH from about 3 to 12 against 0 to 40 mL of base. It starts at pH 2.87, rises gently through the buffer region, passes pH 4.74 at 12.5 mL, the marked answer, and jumps to pH 8.72 at 25 mL, the equivalence point.
visual.caption: Three of the choices are landmarks on this curve: start, halfway and equivalence. Only halfway answers the question.
